text:
customer_jane: Hey Redwood, since ~08:30 UTC our agents in customer-vpc keep failing to register with the Private control plane. Errors in logs look like: 

customer-agent: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = tls: unknown certificate authority

customer_jane: It started after a routine fw rule push on our edge. We can reach the control plane IP but mTLS completes only ~30% of the time. Any quick checks?

support_bot: Thanks for reporting — assigning to @alex and @priya. Please attach a packet capture and an openssl s_client output if possible.

alex: Can you run an s_client from one of the failing hosts showing the client cert handshake? Example we usually ask for: 

```
openssl s_client -connect cp.customer-vpc.redwood:443 -servername cp.customer-vpc.redwood \
  -cert client.pem -key client.key -showcerts -CAfile ca_bundle.pem
```

alex: Also a short tcpdump filtered on port 443 while reproducing would help (capture 3-5 handshakes).

customer_jane: Attached a small capture and here's the s_client output (redacted):

```
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=0 CN = cp.customer-vpc.redwood
verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
verify return:1
---
Certificate chain
 0 s:/CN=cp.customer-vpc.redwood
   i:/CN=Intermediate-CA
 1 s:/CN=Intermediate-CA
   i:/CN=Root-CA
---
---
SSL handshake has read 4021 bytes and written 1234 bytes
---
Verify return code: 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate)
```

priya: That Verify code 20 on s_client from the client side usually means the client couldn't verify the server chain. But you said the control plane rejects the client cert (tls: unknown certificate authority). We need to see the server's perception. From the control plane logs we see: 

"tls: client certificate verify failed: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority"

priya: Can you run an s_client to the control plane WITHOUT client cert and `-showcerts` so we can inspect the server's cert chain ordering as presented to clients? 

customer_jane: Ran this and pasted output: 

```
$ openssl s_client -connect cp.customer-vpc.redwood:443 -servername cp.customer-vpc.redwood -showcerts
---
Certificate chain
0 s:/CN=cp.customer-vpc.redwood
  i:/CN=Intermediate-CA
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIC... (leaf)
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
1 s:/CN=Root-CA
  i:/CN=Intermediate-CA
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIF... (root)
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
2 s:/CN=Intermediate-CA
  i:/CN=Root-CA
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIE... (intermediate)
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
---
```

priya: Ah — the chain being sent is leaf -> root -> intermediate. That ordering is suspicious. Standard expectation is leaf -> intermediate(s) -> root (or leaf -> intermediate... without sending root). Some TLS stacks tolerate odd ordering, but our control plane's mutual TLS verification code expects the intermediate immediately after the leaf to build the chain. If a proxy or TLS-inspect device reorders the chain, verification can fail.

alex: Also saw in the tcpdump you uploaded that the Certificate message length is larger than typical and the server_hello is followed by a TLS inspector. The packet shows `TLS-inspect: re-signed by Enterprise-Proxy`. Are you running a TLS inspection appliance (BlueCoat / Symantec / F5 ASM) at egress?

customer_jane: Yes — we route egress through a BlueCoat proxy for corporate inspection. We recently upgraded it last week (v9.2.4). Vendor says they do "certificate re-sign" for inspected flows.

vendor_mark: From BlueCoat side: there's a known regression in 9.2.4 where the proxy emits the cert chain in a non-standard order when re-signing with a local intermediate. We can reproduce the chain order leaf->root->intermediate. Patch planned.

alex: That matches. When the proxy re-signs it seems to insert the root cert immediately after the leaf, then append the real intermediate. Our control plane TLS verifier treats the next cert after leaf as the signing issuer and fails to construct the chain when order is wrong.

priya: Short-term workaround: add a firewall exception so traffic to cp.customer-vpc.redwood goes direct (bypass TLS-inspect) or configure the proxy to not perform TLS inspection for that hostname. Long-term: vendor patch.

customer_jane: We disabled TLS inspection for cp.customer-vpc.redwood on the proxy (bypassed inspection) and retried — agent registration immediately recovered and errors disappeared.

customer_jane: Quick evidence — new s_client output after bypass: 

```
Verify return code: 0 (ok)
Certificate chain
0 s:/CN=cp.customer-vpc.redwood
  i:/CN=Intermediate-CA
1 s:/CN=Intermediate-CA
  i:/CN=Root-CA
---
```

alex: Great. That confirms the proxy was mutating the cert chain. We'll mark this as root cause: egress TLS-inspect appliance re-sign produced non-standard cert chain ordering, causing control plane mTLS client cert verification to fail.

priya: We recommend: 1) keep the bypass for control plane hostnames, 2) ask vendor for patch, 3) if you need inspection, configure proxy to send full chain in correct order (leaf->intermediates).

customer_jane: Will schedule vendor patch and keep bypass in place for now. Thanks both. :thumbsup:

alex: Closing this thread. If anything recurs ping us and include a fresh capture.

support_bot: Incident closed (linked ticket #CS-4723)"
